yat-nam.name: Pouring the water
yat-nam.one_line: Pour a thin stream of water while the chanting runs, and say who it is for.
how: Buy or borrow a small jug. Any bottle does.
While a monk chants, pour a thread of water — slow, unbroken — into a cup, a bowl, or onto the ground at the foot of a tree.
Hold the dead person in mind and name them, silently or aloud.
When the chanting stops, tip the rest out at the root of a tree.
yat-nam.words: อิทัง เม ญาตีนัง โหตุ — let this be for my relatives.
yat-nam.note: This is the act that moves merit from you to someone dead. Every other act on this page ends with it.

tan-khan-khao.name: Tan khan khao — the tray of rice
tan-khan-khao.th: ตานขันข้าว
tan-khan-khao.nth: ตานขันเข้า
tan-khan-khao.one_line: A tray of food handed to a monk in a named dead person's name.
how: Make up or buy a tray: rice, a savoury dish, a sweet, water, sometimes a flower, a candle and incense.
Write the dead person's name on a slip and put it on the tray, or tell the monk.
Hand it over in the morning, before the monks eat — before about 11 a.m.
The monk chants; you pour the water.
tan-khan-khao.cost: 50–200 ฿ for a tray bought at the wat gate. Made at home it costs what the food costs.
tan-khan-khao.when: Any morning. Most households do it at Pi Mai Mueang (Songkran), at Ok Phansa, and on the anniversary of a death.
tan-khan-khao.note: The Lanna form. In the north this, not the incense stick, is what people mean by making merit for the dead.

tan-tung.name: Offering a tung
tan-tung.one_line: A long narrow banner, raised at the wat, offered in a dead person's name.
how: Buy a tung at the wat or at Ton Lam Yai market — paper, cloth, or metal.
Write the name on the tail.
Hand it to the wat to be hung, or hang it on the pole yourself where the wat puts them.
tan-tung.cost: 20–150 ฿ paper or cloth. A metal one runs higher.
tan-tung.note: The northern telling is that the banner hangs down far enough for the dead to take hold of and climb.

pang-pratip.name: Lighting a pang pratip
pang-pratip.one_line: A small clay saucer with a wick, lit at the base of a chedi.
how: Buy a handful at the wat or at any market in the weeks before Yi Peng.
Fill with wax or oil if it is not already filled; light it; set it down on the terrace, the wall, or the chedi's base.
Do not leave it where it can catch.
pang-pratip.when: Any time. In quantity at Yi Peng, on the full moon of the twelfth northern month.
pang-pratip.note: The lamps are for the dark, and the dark is where the dead are said to be.

bangsukun.name: Pha bangsukun — the cloth
bangsukun.th: ผ้าบังสุกุล
bangsukun.one_line: A length of cloth laid out for a monk to take up, on behalf of someone dead.
how: Ask at the wat office for บังสุกุล. Bring a robe-length of cloth, or buy one there.
Lay it where the monk directs — over a coffin, a photograph, a reliquary, or a bare mat.
The monk takes it up and chants the four lines about what is impermanent.
bangsukun.note: The oldest of these acts and the plainest: a rag picked up off the ground, which is what the word means.

khan-tang.name: Khan tang — the tray for a spirit
khan-tang.nth: ขันห้า / ขันแปด
khan-tang.one_line: Paired flowers and candles on a tray, set down in front of a spirit or a teacher.
how: Count in pairs. Five pairs of flowers and five pairs of candles is the small tray; eight pairs is the larger one.
Add betel, a little rice, a coin.
Set it down, kneel, say what you came for. Take the tray away with you or leave it, as the shrine keeper directs.
khan-tang.cost: 30–150 ฿ ready-made at the shrine. Less if you assemble it.
khan-tang.note: This one is not Buddhist merit. It is what you hand a spirit who was here before the wats were, and it is what the shrines on this route are actually set up to receive.

khan-dok.name: Sai khan dok — flowers in the bowl
khan-dok.one_line: Drop flowers into each of the bowls set out around the pillar.
how: Take a bunch from the sellers at the gate.
Walk the row of bowls and put a few blooms in each.
Some bowls carry a name — a guardian, a direction, a year of birth. Read the labels.
khan-dok.when: The eight days of Bun Inthakhin, ending on the full moon of the eighth northern month (late May). Outside those days the bowls are not out.
khan-dok.note: For the city pillar, not for a person.

suep-chata.name: Suep chata — extending the thread
suep-chata.one_line: A rite that lengthens a life, a house, a river or a town.
how: Arranged with the wat in advance, not walked into.
A tripod of poles, banana stems, a thread that runs from the chanting down to whoever is sitting under it.
suep-chata.note: Listed here because two of the stops on this route are places where the rite is done for the whole city, not for a person.

song-khro.name: Song khro — sending it away
song-khro.th: ส่งเคราะห์
song-khro.one_line: Misfortune loaded onto a raft or a tray and carried out of the house.
how: A tray or a small raft, a scrap of the person's clothing or hair, rice, a figure standing in for them.
Set down at a crossroads, a river, or outside the wall — outward, always.
Done by a spirit doctor or a lay elder rather than by a monk.
song-khro.note: The old city gates were the outward. Suan Prung was the one the dead went through.

unclaimed.name: Paying for the unclaimed dead
unclaimed.th: ทำบุญศพไร้ญาติ
unclaimed.one_line: Money to the rescue foundation that collects bodies nobody claims, and buries or burns them.
how: Chiang Mai's foundations keep a donation box at their stations and take transfers.
Ask for ศพไร้ญาติ — the unclaimed.
Some years a foundation holds a mass cremation for the year's accumulated dead and takes names then.
unclaimed.note: For a route about people who died without anyone to light a lamp for them, this is the act that matches.

sweep.name: Sweeping
sweep.th: กวาดลานวัด
sweep.one_line: Pick up a broom that is already leaning there and sweep.
how: Brooms sit against the wall at most of these wats.
Sweep the terrace, the path, the leaf fall under the bodhi tree. Put the broom back.
sweep.note: Counts. Nobody will stop you, and at the quiet wats on this route it is the most useful thing a visitor does all day.

tile.name: Buying a tile
tile.th: ทำบุญกระเบื้อง
tile.one_line: Write a name on a roof tile that goes onto a building.
how: Where a wat is re-roofing there is a stack of tiles and a marker pen.
Write the dead person's name, your own, or both.
Pay what the sign asks and set the tile on the pile.
tile.cost: Usually 50–100 ฿ a tile; the sign says.
tile.note: Only available where there is work going on. Two or three of these stops have a stack out at any given time.
